text: I think many of us do. I know people who can't get to a friend's flat without their phone, even after visiting it several times. The apps are incredibly useful, but they make us follow instructions instead of noticing where we are. So when the battery dies or there's no signal, people feel completely helpless in places they should know well.

questions.question: Do people rely too much on GPS and map apps?

text: Probably a bit of both. Some people seem naturally good at remembering routes, but I believe practice matters more. Taxi drivers who learn a city without apps develop an amazing mental map. Anyone could improve by walking without a phone now and then, paying attention to landmarks and trying to work out the route before checking it.

tips.en: A bit of both, but practice matters more is not avoiding the question.

text: Clear signs in more than one language are the most obvious step, especially near stations and tourist sites. Free maps at airports still help people whose phones don't work abroad. I also like the idea of numbered walking routes, like in some European cities, where you just follow coloured lines on the pavement. In Almaty, the mountains help, because they're always in the south.

text: In most situations, yes. The vast majority of people are happy to help, and some, like the man who helped me in Istanbul, go out of their way to do it. Of course, it makes sense to be careful — for example, to ask people in shops or at information desks rather than someone who approaches you first. But I think fear of strangers is often exaggerated.

text: It really depends on the city and the child, but I'd say around eleven or twelve for short, familiar journeys, like the way to school. Children who never go anywhere alone often lack confidence later. Parents can start gradually — first walking the route together, then following at a distance — and giving the child a phone for emergencies.

tips.en: Around eleven or twelve for short, familiar journeys is a precise answer with a condition.
